clinicalPearls: Chronic venous disease spans a spectrum: telangiectasias and reticular veins, to varicose veins, to chronic venous insufficiency with edema, skin changes, and ulceration (p.2179).

Chronic venous insufficiency arises from incompetent veins with venous hypertension and extravasation of fluid and blood elements into the limb; it may occur with superficial venous disease, but more advanced manifestations are usually caused by deep-vein disease (p.2180).

Secondary deep-venous insufficiency most often follows deep-vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic syndrome): valve leaflets become thickened and contracted, losing the ability to prevent retrograde flow, and the vein wall becomes rigid and thick-walled (p.2180).
Lipodermatosclerosis is the combination of induration, hemosiderin deposition, and inflammation, typically in the lower leg just above the ankle (the gaiter area) (p.2180).
Atrophie blanche is a white patch of scar tissue, often with focal telangiectasias and a hyperpigmented border, usually developing near the medial malleolus (p.2180).
A venous ulcer is typically shallow with an irregular border, a base of granulation tissue, and exudate, and occurs near the medial and lateral malleoli (p.2180).
Venous edema is usually pitting early on, but over time may become less pitting and more indurated, particularly with secondary development of lymphatic dysfunction (phlebolymphedema) (p.2180).

Lymphedema is generally a painless condition; it initially involves the foot and progresses up the leg, with early soft pitting edema that later becomes nonpitting with a woody, indurated, fibrotic texture (p.2183-2184).
Stemmer's sign (inability to tent the skin at the base of the toes) and peau d'orange (orange-peel dimpling), along with squaring of the toes, are characteristic skin findings of lymphedema (p.2184).
Worldwide, the most common cause of secondary lymphedema is lymphatic filariasis; in developed countries it is surgical excision or irradiation of axillary/inguinal lymph nodes for cancer (p.2183).
Recurrent bacterial lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, is a very common cause of lymphedema, and lymphedema in turn predisposes to recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis - a vicious cycle (p.2183-2184).
harrison.pathophysiology: In chronic venous disease, incompetent (refluxing) or obstructed veins produce sustained venous hypertension with extravasation of fluid and blood elements into limb tissues. Primary varicose veins arise from defective saphenous valves, intrinsic vein-wall weakness, and high intraluminal pressure; secondary varicosities and chronic venous insufficiency result from deep-venous obstruction or valvular incompetence, classically post-thrombotic (valve leaflets thicken and contract after DVT, the vein becomes rigid, and distal valves become incompetent as high pressure distends the vein). Other secondary causes include May-Thurner syndrome, extrinsic compression by tumor/retroperitoneal fibrosis, arteriovenous fistulas, deep-vein agenesis, and venous malformations. Lymphedema results from impaired lymph transport: deficiency, reflux, or obstruction of lymph vessels causes an imbalance between lymph production and absorption (governed by Starling forces), so protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitium and raises tissue osmotic load. Persistent lymphedema triggers inflammatory/immune responses with infiltration of mononuclear cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes, leading to adipose and collagen deposition in skin and subcutaneous tissues (p.2180, 2182-2183).
additionalDifferentials: Hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic syndrome or severe hepatic disease
Myxedema from hypothyroidism, or pretibial myxedema with Graves' disease
Drug-induced edema (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones)
Lipedema (adipose accumulation thigh-to-ankle sparing the feet, usually in women)
Ruptured leg muscle, hematoma from trauma, popliteal (Baker's) cyst (unilateral swelling)
infectionMimics: Cellulitis (erythema and swelling of the affected limb)
nonInfectiousMimics: Lymphedema vs chronic venous insufficiency (venous edema is softer with stasis dermatitis, hyperpigmentation, and superficial varicosities)
Lipedema (spares the feet; differentiated by MRI)

Leg ulcers from severe peripheral artery disease / chronic limb-threatening ischemia, diabetic neuropathy, skin cancer, vasculitis, or rarely hydroxyurea (distinct from venous ulcers by location and characteristics)
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasonography - principal test; detects obstruction (no flow, echogenic thrombus, non-compressible vein) and reflux (prolonged flow reversal on Valsalva or cuff release)
Air/strain-gauge plethysmography to quantify venous reflux and calf-muscle-pump efficiency
MR, CT, or conventional venography for suspected IVC/iliofemoral obstruction, IVC filter occlusion, extrinsic compression, or May-Thurner syndrome
Bedside Brodie-Trendelenburg test (deep vs superficial reflux) and Perthes test (deep-venous obstruction) - now used infrequently
For lymphedema: abdominal/pelvic ultrasound and CT for obstructing neoplasm; MRI of the limb (honeycomb epifascial pattern; distinguishes lipedema)
Lymphoscintigraphy and lymphangiography (rarely needed) to confirm and distinguish primary from secondary lymphedema
Near-infrared fluorescence optical imaging for quantitative superficial lymph-flow assessment, useful operatively
redFlags: Acute unilateral leg swelling raising concern for deep-vein thrombosis (duration of edema helps distinguish DVT from chronic venous insufficiency)
Suspected proximal venous obstruction (IVC/iliofemoral) warranting intervention
Infected or rapidly worsening venous ulcer
Lymphangiosarcoma - a rare but highly lethal complication of long-standing uncontrolled lymphedema
Recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis in a lymphedematous limb
harrison.prognosis: Approximately 20% of patients with chronic venous insufficiency develop venous ulcers. Recurrent varicose veins occur in up to 50% of patients by 5 years after ligation and stripping. Endovenous thermal ablation achieves 1- and 5-year occlusion rates exceeding ~90%; sclerotherapy averages ~81% and ~74% at 1 and 5 years. Iliac venous stenting has technical success >85% with long-term patency ~75%; venous bypass long-term patency generally exceeds 60%. Lymphedema is a chronic, generally progressive condition; failure to control limb edema may lead to recurrent infections, progressive trophic skin changes, and rarely the highly lethal complication of lymphangiosarcoma (p.2179, 2182-2184).
pitfalls: Lymphedema is often confused with chronic venous insufficiency, and the two can coexist as phlebolymphedema when venous insufficiency impairs lymphatic function - do not assume a single cause (p.2180).
Distinguish bilateral venous edema and lymphedema from systemic causes (heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, myxedema, drug-induced edema) before attributing swelling to venous disease (p.2180).
Distinguish unilateral leg swelling of chronic venous insufficiency/lymphedema from acute deep-vein thrombosis - the duration of edema helps differentiate them (p.2180, 2183).
Compression garments improve symptoms and aid ulcer healing but are NOT curative and do NOT prevent progression of varicose veins (p.2181).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for a venous ulcer unless it is infected (p.2181).
Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema - they may cause intravascular volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities (p.2184).
No drugs are FDA-approved for chronic venous insufficiency, and there is insufficient evidence to recommend general use of venoactive herbal supplements (p.2182).
harrison.severityClassification: CEAP (Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic) classification of chronic venous disease. Clinical: C0 no signs; C1 telangiectasias/reticular veins; C2 varicose veins (C2r recurrent); C3 edema; C4 skin/subcutaneous changes (C4a pigmentation or eczema, C4b lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche, C4c corona phlebectatica); C5 healed venous ulcer; C6 active venous ulcer (C6r recurrent). Etiologic: Ep primary, Es secondary (Esi intravenous, Ese extravenous), Ec congenital, En none identified. Anatomic: As superficial, Ap perforator, Ad deep, An none. Pathophysiologic: Pr reflux, Po obstruction, Pr,o both, Pn none. Lymphedema is staged by the International Society of Lymphology: Stage 0/Ia latent/subclinical; Stage I early protein-rich edema reduced by elevation, may pit; Stage II elevation rarely reduces swelling, pitting manifest then later non-pitting as fat/fibrosis supervene; Stage III lymphostatic elephantiasis with trophic skin changes, acanthosis, fat/fibrosis, warty overgrowths (p.2181, 2184).
references: Harrison 22e Chapter 293: Chronic Venous Disease and Lymphedema (Creager, Eberhardt, Loscalzo)
